references.text: Isaiah urges God's people not to fear mortal humans: 'Do not be afraid of human mockery, do not be terrified by their taunts. For the moth will eat them like a garment' (Jes 51:7-8). The same principle as in Luke 12:4 – humans can only harm the body, nothing more.

The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says: 'Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul' (Matt 10:28). This is the closest parallel to Luke 12:4, with almost identical wording.
Jesus encourages the disciples not to fear because they are worth more than many sparrows (Matt 10:31). The context is the same exhortation not to fear humans.
Peter and the apostles say: 'We must obey God rather than humans' (Acts 5:29). They demonstrated in practice that they did not fear those who could kill the body, but feared God more.
'The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can a human do to me?' (Heb 13:6). The same fundamental attitude as in Jesus' words: humans cannot do anything beyond physical harm.

Peter writes: 'But even if you should suffer for doing what is right, you are blessed. Do not fear their threats or be frightened' (1 Pet 3:14). A direct exhortation not to fear human persecution, in line with Jesus' words in Luke 12:4.
'There is no fear in love. Perfect love drives out fear' (1 John 4:18). Love for God overcomes the fear of humans who can only kill the body.

Jesus says to the church in Smyrna: 'Do not be afraid of what you are about to suffer ... Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life' (Rev 2:10). An exhortation not to fear persecution and physical death, consistent with Luke 12:4.

David says: 'All day long they twist my words; all their thoughts are against me for evil. ... What can a human do to me?' (Ps 56:5). Expresses the confidence that God's people need not fear what humans can do.
Jesus calls his disciples friends (John 15:13-15), which corresponds to Jesus' address 'my friends' (τοῖς φίλοις μου) in Luke 12:4. Jesus uses the concept of friendship for his disciples.
